digest.top_line: Gomez LCT, oligometastatic NSCLC: mOS 41.2 vs 17.0 mo (P = .017) with RT/surgery to all sites after first-line therapy; randomized phase II stopped early at N=49.
digest.tldr: Oligomets and gyn carried the day. In NSCLC with ≤3 mets and no progression on first-line therapy, LCT more than doubled mOS (41.2 vs 17.0 mo), though the trial stopped early for benefit. In the PORTEC-3 final analysis, adding chemo to pelvic RT improved 5y FFS (HR 0.71) but not OS (HR 0.76, ns), with G3+ AEs at 60% vs 12%.

sites.intro: Two brachy planning studies (eBT OAR sparing vs replanned Ir-192, cylinder tip-space dosimetry) sit beside PORTEC-3; neither reports late clinical toxicity.

studies.name: PORTEC-3
studies.tldr: Adding chemo to pelvic RT: 5y FFS 75.5% vs 68.6% (HR 0.71, p=0.022); 5y OS 81.8% vs 76.7%, HR 0.76, ns.
details: 🔍 Open-label randomised phase 3, 103 centres, GCIG intergroup
🔍 686 enrolled, 660 eligible pts in final ITT analysis (330 per arm)
🔍 Median f/u 60.2 mo (IQR 48.1-73.1)

subdetails: Stage IA endometrioid grade 3 with LVSI
Serous or clear cell, stage IA (with invasion) to III

details: 💊 RT both arms: pelvic EBRT 48.6 Gy in 1.8 Gy fractions
💊 CRT arm: cisplatin 50 mg/m² x2 during RT, then carboplatin AUC5 + paclitaxel 175 mg/m² x4
🔍 Vaginal brachy boost in 47% (46% CRT vs 48% RT), mostly for cervical invasion

details.text: 📊 5y outcomes, CRT vs RT alone (prose-reported values)

details: 📊 Pelvic control 91% with RT alone
⚠️ G3+ AEs during treatment 60% CRT vs 12% RT (p<0.0001)
⚠️ G2+ neuropathy persisting at 3y: 8% vs 1% (p<0.0001)
⚠️ OS underpowered: 136 OS events, 69% of required; time-based final analysis
⚠️ Stage III FFS gain is a subgroup read, hypothesis-generating
🔗 Consistent with pooled NSGO-EC-9501/EORTC-55991 + MaNGO Iliade (PFS 78% vs 69%, p=0.01)

verdict.rationale: Randomised phase 3 hit co-primary FFS but not OS, with OS events short of target. Aligns with pooled NSGO/EORTC/Iliade direction; toxicity cost tempers adoption below stage III.
verdict.audience: High-risk endometrial cancer, FIGO 2009 stage I-III, post-hysterectomy

studies.significance: Pelvic RT alone already held pelvic control at 91%, so the chemo gain is a distant-failure question, not a local one. The FFS gain concentrates in stage III (69.3% vs 58.0%, HR 0.66), while stage I-II FFS HR 0.85 was ns, supporting RT alone below stage III.
studies.monday_clinic: In stage III high-risk endometrial cancer after surgery, this supports counselling on concurrent plus adjuvant chemo with pelvic RT for FFS; it does not establish an OS gain, nor a meaningful benefit in stage I-II disease.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Open-label randomised phase 3**, 1:1, 103 centres across six GCIG groups. Biased-coin minimisation stratified by centre, lymphadenectomy, stage and histology. **Median follow-up 60.2 mo**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **High-risk endometrial cancer, FIGO 2009**: endometrioid grade 3 stage I with deep invasion and/or LVSI, endometrioid stage II-III, or serous/clear cell stage I-III. Median age 62; stage III in 46% CRT vs 43% RT.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **Pelvic EBRT 48.6 Gy in 1.8 Gy fractions** both arms; 329 (100%) CRT and 322 (98%) RT pts received 45.0-50.4 Gy. Vaginal brachy boost in 47%, balanced across arms.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: CRT arm added **cisplatin 50 mg/m² x2 concurrent**, then **carboplatin AUC5 + paclitaxel 175 mg/m² x4**. Both cisplatin cycles completed by 92%; all four carboplatin cycles by 79%, paclitaxel by 71%.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Co-primary: overall survival and failure-free survival**, ITT, Cox adjusted for stratification factors.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **G3+ AEs during treatment 60% vs 12%** (p<0.0001). G2+ neuropathy persisted at 3y in **8% vs 1%**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Direction matches the pooled **NSGO-EC-9501/EORTC-55991 + MaNGO Iliade** analysis (PFS 78% vs 69%, OS trend 82% vs 75%). RT-alone pelvic control of 91% echoes **GOG-249**, where chemo plus vaginal brachy did not beat pelvic EBRT and pelvic/para-aortic failures rose.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents surgically staged or hysterectomised high-risk endometrial cancer, FIGO 2009 stage I-III, fit for platinum. Does not represent stage IV disease or pts unfit for combined chemo.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Event rates ran below design assumptions, so OS reached **69% of required events** and the 5% OS gap was smaller than the trial was powered to detect. Stage and histology benefit estimates rest on subgroups with limited events.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Chemo buys distant control, not pelvic control, at a real toxicity cost. Authors judge the stage I-II FFS gain **not worth the toxicity**, and the stage III 11% absolute FFS gain clinically relevant; OS remains unsettled pending longer follow-up.

studies.interpretation:
The cleanest way to read PORTEC-3 is as a trial about distant failure in a population where pelvic RT already does its job. Pelvic control was 91% with radiotherapy alone, so there was little local headroom for chemotherapy to claim, and the FFS improvement (HR 0.71) has to come predominantly from fewer distant events. That framing matters for how a radiation oncologist uses it: the trial does not argue that RT is insufficient locally; it argues that a subset of high-risk pts carries enough systemic risk that adding platinum-taxane changes their failure-free trajectory.

The OS result should be read for what it is rather than as a negative. The trial accrued fully, but event rates were lower than assumed at design, and the time-based final analysis captured 136 OS events, 69% of the required number. A 5% OS difference with an upper CI bound of 1.06 is compatible with a modest real benefit that this analysis could not resolve. Equally, it is compatible with no benefit, and a reader should not borrow confidence from the FFS result to fill that gap. The authors' own call for continued follow-up is the honest position.

Against prior data, the result is consistent rather than surprising. The pooled NSGO-EC-9501/EORTC-55991 and MaNGO Iliade analysis, using sequential platinum chemotherapy with pelvic RT, showed the same direction on PFS and a similar OS trend, in a population with only about 20% stage III disease. RTOG 9708, the phase 2 schedule PORTEC-3 adopted, reported 4-year OS of 85%, in the same range as the 82% seen here. GOG-249 is the useful counterweight: in stage I-II high-intermediate and high-risk disease, replacing pelvic EBRT with chemo plus vaginal brachy offered no superiority and more pelvic and para-aortic failure. Read together, those trials suggest pelvic RT is the anchor for locoregional control and chemotherapy is an addition whose value scales with systemic risk. GOG-258, comparing this CRT schedule with chemo alone, was only presented at the time, but its reported excess of vaginal and pelvic or para-aortic recurrence without RT points the same way.

The stage split is where decisions actually get made, and also where confidence should be most guarded. Stage III pts gained FFS 69.3% vs 58.0% (HR 0.66), while stage I-II FFS was 80.8% vs 76.6% with a CI spanning 1. Stage was a stratification factor, which strengthens the subgroup somewhat, but the trial was not powered within strata. The age signal, larger benefit at 70 and older, is more fragile still, and the authors themselves raise selection of fitter older women.

Toxicity is not a footnote here. G3+ AEs ran 60% vs 12%, and persistent neuropathy at 3 years was 8% vs 1%. For stage I-II pts with high baseline FFS, that cost is hard to justify on this evidence. For stage III, the absolute FFS gain exceeds the 10% the trial was designed around. What would make the stage III read wrong is an OS that never separates with longer follow-up, or a molecular stratification showing the benefit is confined to a subset that stage alone only approximates.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Pelvic control was 91% with 48.6 Gy pelvic EBRT alone, so chemo does not add local value. Stage I-II FFS HR 0.85 (p=0.47) supports RT alone there; stage III is where adding systemic therapy earns its toxicity.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Concurrent cisplatin plus 4 cycles carboplatin/paclitaxel improved FFS (HR 0.71) at a cost of G3+ AEs 60% vs 12% and persistent G2+ neuropathy 8% vs 1% at 3y. Only 79% completed all carboplatin cycles; stage III carries the absolute benefit.

open_questions: Does OS separate with longer follow-up?
Chemo alone vs CRT in stage III disease
Benefit in serous and clear cell histology

studies.name: Axxent electronic brachytherapy, postoperative endometrial cancer
studies.tldr: eBT cut bladder V35% 15.2% vs 28.2% and rectal V35% 16.7% vs 32% vs replanned Ir-192, with 1 acute G2 event in 94 pts.
details: 🔍 Single-centre series, N=94, Sept 2015 to Oct 2017, Axxent 50 kVp eBT via vaginal cylinder

subdetails: eBT exclusive: 37 pts, 25 Gy in 5 sessions (stage IA plus 7 IB1)
EBRT + eBT: 57 pts, whole pelvis 23 × 2 Gy, then eBT 15 Gy in 3 sessions
Prescribed at 5 mm from applicator; PTV = active length + 5 mm
Cylinders 2.5 to 3.5 cm diameter; eBT twice weekly

details: 🔍 Each eBT plan replanned a posteriori for Ir-192 and Co-60: 282 plans, TG-43, no heterogeneity correction

details.text: 📐 Mean OAR dose, eBT vs replanned Ir-192 HDR

details: 📊 Co-60 plan OAR doses similar to Ir-192
📊 PTV V150/V200 higher with eBT; gap narrows as cylinder size increases
📊 Acute toxicity: only 1 event above G1 (G2, RTOG) across 94 pts

details.text: 📊 No recurrence in 31 pts past 12 mo (median f/u 19 mo, range 12-25)

details: ⚠️ No RBE correction applied; cited 50 kV RBE vs Ir-192 is 1.29 to 1.85 at 5 mm
⚠️ Comparator plans recalculated, never delivered; no clinical HDR control cohort
⚠️ Late vaginal toxicity (stenosis) not reported; f/u 14 mo (4-25)

details.text: ⚠️ Internal inconsistencies: 30 vs 31 pts with 12-mo f/u; average energy 26 vs 29.6 keV

verdict.rationale: Single-centre uncontrolled series, N=94, 14-mo f/u; OAR comparison is replanned physical dose without RBE correction, and cuff control rests on 31 pts past 12 mo.
verdict.audience: Postoperative endometrial cancer, FIGO IA-IVA, adjuvant vaginal cuff brachy

studies.significance: The OAR savings are TG-43 physical dose with no RBE correction, while PTV V150/V200 rose with eBT, most with the smallest cylinder. Against a cited 50 kV RBE of 1.29 to 1.85 vs Ir-192 at 5 mm, the biologic mucosal dose is unknown, which matters most for 2.5 cm cylinders and the 25 Gy/5 fx exclusive schedule.
studies.monday_clinic: In a centre without an HDR afterloader treating postoperative endometrial cancer with vaginal cuff brachytherapy, this supports 50 kV eBT as feasible on acute toxicity; it does not establish equivalent cuff control or late vaginal toxicity vs Ir-192 HDR.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Single-centre series of **94 pts** treated Sept 2015 to Oct 2017 with Axxent eBT. Each delivered plan was **replanned a posteriori** for Ir-192 and Co-60 (282 plans) under TG-43 for a dosimetric comparison; toxicity scored by RTOG.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Postoperative endometrial cancer, FIGO IA through IVA; mean age 65.9 (33-84). **33 pts (35%)** received chemotherapy before RT.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **Exclusive eBT 25 Gy in 5 sessions** (37 pts) or **whole-pelvis EBRT 23 × 2 Gy then eBT 15 Gy in 3 sessions** (57 pts). Dose prescribed at 5 mm from cylinders of 2.5 to 3.5 cm; **no RBE adjustment** for the 50 kVp beam.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Bladder, rectum and sigmoid D2cc, V50% and V35%; PTV V150/V200; acute, 1-month and 12-month RTOG toxicity. Recurrence reported descriptively.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Only **1 acute event above G1** (G2). At 1 month, vaginal G0 94.7% and G1 5.3%, with G2 cases resolved.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Adjuvant vaginal cuff HDR with Ir-192 is the reference technique, and PORTEC-2 is the trial that set VBT as the adjuvant standard for high-intermediate risk disease. The source cites a multicentre eBT series with bladder V50% 11.5 ± 9.7% and rectum 17.4 ± 10.9%, same direction as here.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents postoperative endometrial cancer receiving vaginal cuff cylinder brachytherapy alone or as a boost after whole-pelvis EBRT. Does not represent late toxicity outcomes, RBE-adjusted eBT prescriptions, or cervix applications.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: **TG-43 without heterogeneity correction** understates the tissue-composition effect at 50 kV, where the authors themselves cite Monte-Carlo recommendations. Reporting is internally inconsistent on follow-up (mean vs median 14 mo; 30 vs 31 pts past 12 mo) and source energy.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The steeper falloff of a 50 kV source predictably lowers distal OAR dose while raising the mucosal hot spot; the open question is whether that hot spot, carrying higher RBE, costs late vaginal toxicity. **Acute toxicity alone cannot answer it**, and cuff recurrence is too rare to judge at this follow-up.

studies.interpretation:
The dosimetric finding here is close to a physical certainty rather than a discovery. A 50 kVp source deposits dose with a much steeper gradient than Ir-192, so when both plans are normalised to the same depth 5 mm from the cylinder surface, the low-energy plan will deliver less dose to bladder and rectum a few centimetres away and more dose to the vaginal mucosa sitting against the applicator. The paper shows exactly that pattern: lower D2cc, V50% and V35% for every OAR, and higher PTV V150 and V200, with the hot-spot excess shrinking as the cylinder diameter grows. The question a brachytherapist actually needs answered is not whether the OAR numbers fall, but whether the mucosal trade is clinically free.

On that question the series is weaker than its conclusions suggest. Prescriptions were not adjusted for relative biological effectiveness, and the authors themselves cite estimates of 1.29 to 1.85 relative to Ir-192 at 5 mm, alongside Rava et al., whose BED modelling at an RBE of 1.5 implied higher mucosal dose. If those estimates are anywhere near right, the delivered biologic dose at the cuff surface exceeds the HDR equivalent, and the OAR comparison, computed in physical dose under TG-43 without heterogeneity correction, flatters eBT. The low acute and 1-month toxicity is reassuring but not discriminating: vaginal cuff HDR is itself a low-toxicity procedure acutely, and the endpoint that would expose an excess mucosal dose is late, namely stenosis, shortening and dryness, which is not reported.

The efficacy signal is thinner still. No recurrences among the roughly 30 pts followed beyond a year says little in a population where vaginal cuff failure after adjuvant brachytherapy is uncommon to begin with. The cohort is also heterogeneous, mixing exclusive brachytherapy for early-stage disease with boosts after whole-pelvis EBRT and chemotherapy in a third of pts, so any cuff control observation is diluted across very different risk groups. PORTEC-2 is what made vaginal brachytherapy the adjuvant standard for high-intermediate risk disease, and that standard was built on conventional HDR sources; transferring it to a 50 kV source is a claim of biologic equivalence the present data cannot carry.

Where the result does have practical value is as a feasibility statement for departments without an HDR afterloader or with constrained shielding: the workflow runs, sessions take minutes, and acute toxicity is acceptable. For a centre that already owns Ir-192 HDR, nothing here argues for switching. The decision the data would need to move is whether a 2.5 cm cylinder treated to 25 Gy in 5 fractions with an unadjusted 50 kV prescription is safe for the vaginal mucosa at three to five years, and that requires a prospective cohort with late toxicity scored by validated vaginal instruments, ideally with RBE-informed dose and Monte-Carlo dosimetry. Until then, eBT is an alternative of necessity rather than of equivalence.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The OAR savings are TG-43 physical dose with no RBE correction, while PTV V150/V200 rose with eBT, most with the smallest cylinder. Against a cited RBE of 1.29 to 1.85 vs Ir-192 at 5 mm, biologic mucosal dose is unknown, most relevant for 2.5 cm cylinders and 25 Gy/5 fx exclusive treatment.

open_questions: Late vaginal toxicity with unadjusted 50 kV eBT prescriptions
Vaginal cuff control vs Ir-192 HDR with mature follow-up
RBE-adjusted dose prescription for 50 kV eBT

studies.name: HDR vaginal brachytherapy cylinder dosimetry (depth, size, length, tip space)
studies.tldr: Planning study: dropping optimization points at the cylinder dome gave hot (>150%) and cold (<60%) spots, and shorter tip space raised dosimetric uncertainty >30%.

details.text: 🔍 Dosimetric planning study (Plato BPS 14.2.4), no patient outcomes; single institution (Henry Ford)
🔍 Cylinders 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5 and 4.0 cm diameter; activated lengths 3 to 8 cm
🔍 Compared surface (P0) vs 0.5-cm depth (P5) prescription, each with and without dome optimization points (NEP)
🔍 Tip space: radiographic thin-metal-tube cylinder ~0.5 cm; CT/MR plastic-tube cylinder 0.6 to 0.8 cm on radiograph
📊 Surface vs 0.5-cm depth prescription, surface SD: 6% vs 18% (2-cm cylinder, 0.8-cm tip space)
📊 No-end-point (NEP) plans, 2-cm cylinder, by tip space

rows: Hot spots 140-170% of Rx at surface

details: 📐 Surface conversion factor: M ≈ 1.00 + 0.64 (cm)/L + 1.23 (cm)/S, regression agreement within 2%

details.text: 📐 Worked example: 7 Gy at 0.5 cm, 5-cm length, 3-cm cylinder → M = 1.54 → 10.8 Gy/fx at surface

details: ⚠️ M regression built from only two treatment lengths × two cylinder sizes
⚠️ Toxicity benefit of surface Rx inferred from dose, not measured; no clinical endpoints
🔗 Authors frame surface-dose reduction against Sorbe randomized dose-fractionation trial (mucosal atrophy, bleeding, shortening)

verdict.rationale: Dosimetric planning study with no patient outcomes; the claimed optimal surface prescription and toxicity benefit are inferred from point doses, not tested clinically.
verdict.audience: Post-hysterectomy endometrial cancer, adjuvant HDR vaginal cuff brachytherapy

studies.significance: The dome is where plans fail: omitting optimization points at the curved end swung given dose about 10% in either direction depending on tip space, with apex spots of 50-65% or 140-170%. The M formula (M ≈ 1.00 + 0.64/L + 1.23/S) gives a geometry-specific surface dose matching a 0.5-cm depth Rx, informing the surface-vs-depth prescription choice.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Single-institution **dosimetric planning study** in Plato BPS 14.2.4; no patients treated or followed. Dose uniformity measured as **mean dose (MD) and SD** across dose points spaced evenly around the dome and along the cylinder at each depth.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Single-channel HDR vaginal cylinders **2.0 to 4.0 cm** diameter, activated lengths **3 to 8 cm**. Plans prescribed to the **surface (P0)** or **0.5-cm depth (P5)**, with or without optimization points at the curved end; illustrative Rx 7 Gy × 3.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary metrics:** MD and SD at surface and 0.5-cm depth. Dose fall-off beyond the treatment depth defined as the ratio of MD at 0.75 cm to MD at 0.5 cm.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Surface Rx gave more uniform mucosal dose (**SD 6% vs 18%** at the surface, 2-cm cylinder, 0.8-cm tip space). Shorter tip space raised dosimetric uncertainty **>30%**; plans without dome points produced **hot spots >150% and cold spots <60%**.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents single-channel cylinder HDR VBT planned on point-based optimization with a known tip space. Does not represent multichannel applicators or clinical toxicity outcomes.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: ABS guidance (Nag 2000) already asks for dome optimization points and reporting at both surface and 0.5 cm; this study quantifies what happens when that is skipped. The authors tie surface-dose reduction to the **Sorbe randomized trial**, where the higher dose per fraction increased mucosal atrophy, bleeding and vaginal shortening.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The M formula rests on **two lengths × two cylinder sizes**, then extrapolates. Results are specific to one planning system's optimizer and to the vendor tip-space geometry measured here.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The robust finding is procedural: **dome points must be in the plan**, and tip space has to be known before insertion. The bigger claim, that surface prescription is the **optimal** approach, swaps a mucosal-dose argument for a clinical one that has not been tested.

studies.interpretation:
The paper makes two kinds of claim, and they deserve different levels of trust. The first is a planning-quality claim: a single-channel cylinder plan that ignores the hemispherical dome gives an unpredictable dose at the apex, the site of highest cuff-recurrence concern. That claim is about as secure as a dosimetric result can be. Unlike a clinical question it does not depend on sampling or follow-up, and the direction of the error flips with tip space. With a 0.8-cm tip space the apex ran cold and the given dose fell by about 10%; with a 0.5-cm tip space a surface prescription ran hot at the apex and the given dose rose by about 10%. A planner who leaves out dome points therefore cannot even predict which way the plan is wrong. That is the strongest practical argument in the paper, and it is consistent with what ABS guidance already asked for. It also explains why the authors want the vendor to supply exact applicator geometry and want tip space checked radiographically before treatment.

The second claim is clinical: that prescribing to the surface at a higher dose per fraction is the optimal approach. The data here cannot settle that. The authors show the surface prescription gives a more uniform mucosal dose (surface SD 6% vs 18% in the 2-cm, 0.8-cm tip-space case) with similar coverage and fall-off at 0.5 cm. The step from uniform mucosal dose to fewer complications is borrowed, mainly from the Sorbe randomized dose-fractionation trial, which compared doses per fraction rather than prescription points. Mucosal hot spots are a reasonable mechanism for atrophy, bleeding and shortening, but no patient was treated here, and no dose-toxicity relationship was fitted.

The conversion factor is the part most likely to be used at the console, so its derivation matters. M ≈ 1.00 + 0.64/L + 1.23/S comes from a regression on two treatment lengths and two cylinder sizes, then applied across the 2-4 cm and 3-8 cm range. The stated agreement within 2% is reassuring for the geometries tested. Outside them it is an extrapolation, and it assumes the same optimizer behaviour and tip space. The worked example (7 Gy at 0.5 cm becoming 10.8 Gy at the surface for a 3-cm, 5-cm-length cylinder) shows how steep the conversion is. Many programs that think of their dose as 'the same' under either convention are actually delivering different mucosal doses. Anyone switching convention mid-program should check the mapping in their own planning system, not adopt the coefficients wholesale.

The study also predates image-guided planning becoming routine for vaginal cuff treatment, and it uses point-based optimization in a single commercial system. The procedural lesson carries over to modern practice: dome points matter, tip space matters, and dose should be reported at both surface and depth. What is still open is whether surface prescription actually lowers late vaginal toxicity at matched depth dose. That would take a prospective comparison with vaginal toxicity as a measured endpoint. Until then the paper is a strong argument for disciplined planning and a hypothesis about prescription convention.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The dome is where plans fail: omitting curved-end optimization points swung given dose about 10% either way depending on tip space, with apex spots of 50-65% or 140-170%. The M formula translates a 0.5-cm depth Rx into a geometry-specific surface dose, informing the prescription-point convention.

open_questions: Does surface prescription reduce late vaginal toxicity at matched depth dose?
Does the M conversion factor hold in modern image-guided planning systems?

studies.name: Gomez LCT vs maintenance/observation, oligometastatic NSCLC (long-term OS)
studies.tldr: mOS 41.2 vs 17.0 mo (P = .017) and mPFS 14.2 vs 4.4 mo (P = .022) favoring LCT in oligometastatic NSCLC without progression after first-line therapy.
details: 🔍 Randomized phase II, 3 institutions, 1:1, not masked. 49 randomized of 74 enrolled
🔍 DSMB closed the trial early for PFS benefit. It was powered for 94 randomized pts
🔍 Stage IV NSCLC, ≤3 mets, no progression ≥3 mo after front-line systemic therapy
💊 Front-line therapy: ≥4 cycles platinum doublet, or ≥3 mo EGFR TKI / crizotinib for EGFR/ALK
🔍 LCT: RT or surgery to all active sites, chosen by MDT. Concurrent chemoRT allowed for primary/nodes

details.text: 📊 Efficacy, LCT vs MT/O (median f/u 38.8 mo)

details: 📐 Multivariable OS HR for LCT 0.46 (95% CI 0.21-0.99), P = .048, adjusted for met number + EGFR/ALK
📊 No additional G≥3 toxicity beyond what was previously reported
📊 OS benefit held despite crossover: 9 of 20 MT/O progressors received LCT to all lesions
⚠️ Significance threshold P<.10 (one-sided 10% type I error), so the bar is looser than a phase III
⚠️ Stopped early for benefit at N=49, so the effect size is likely inflated
⚠️ Opened 2012: no immunotherapy. Maintenance regimens were heterogeneous
⚠️ RT dose/fractionation and the RT vs surgery split are not reported in the source

verdict.rationale: Randomized phase II stopped early at N=49 of a planned 94, one-sided alpha 0.10, with OS as a secondary endpoint. Phase III confirmation (NRG-LU002) is still needed.
verdict.audience: Stage IV NSCLC, ≤3 mets, no progression after front-line systemic therapy

studies.significance: Survival after progression ran 37.6 vs 9.4 mo, and only 15 of 39 progressors (41%) received LCT at progression. Holding RT for progression therefore loses a large share of pts who can no longer get consolidation, often from polymetastatic progression (n=7 in MT/O). This argues for consolidating at the post-induction window rather than deferring.
studies.monday_clinic: In stage IV NSCLC with ≤3 mets that has not progressed after ≥4 cycles of platinum doublet or ≥3 mo of first-line TKI, this supports consolidative RT or surgery to all sites over maintenance alone. It does not extend to >3 mets or to disease progressing on front-line therapy.

primary_endpoint.name: Progression-free survival
primary_endpoint.stat_detail: median PFS, P = .022 (α .10); median f/u 38.8 mo

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Randomized phase II**, 1:1, 3 institutions (MD Anderson, London Health Sciences, Colorado), not masked. Randomization was balanced dynamically on five prognostic factors instead of stratified. **Closed early by DSMB** after 49 of 74 enrolled pts were randomized. Median follow-up 38.8 mo.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Stage IV NSCLC (AJCC 7th), ≤3 metastases** excluding the primary, ECOG ≤2, **no progression after standard front-line therapy**: ≥4 cycles platinum doublet, or ≥3 mo erlotinib/EGFR TKI or crizotinib for EGFR/ALK. Adenocarcinoma made up 80% of pts and 94% had synchronous disease. EGFR/ALK n=8.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: LCT was **RT or surgery to all active disease sites**, modality chosen by a multidisciplinary team. Concurrent chemoRT was allowed for the primary and regional nodes. **Dose, fractionation and the RT vs surgery split are not reported in the source.**

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** PFS from randomization. **Secondary:** OS, toxicity, time to new lesions. Imaging was indexed to the enrollment date in both arms, so LCT did not delay scans. P<.10 was deemed significant.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Arm-level efficacy is in the table above. The OS benefit persisted in a multivariable model, **HR 0.46 (0.21-0.99), P = .048**. In an exploratory analysis, initial LCT (HR 0.30, 0.12-0.75) and late LCT (HR 0.44, 0.18-1.06) both correlated with OS.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **No additional grade ≥3 toxicity** beyond events reported in the initial publication.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: This is the source's first randomized OS signal for LCT in lung cancer. It sits alongside SABR-COMET and the UT Southwestern phase II, whose enrolled populations shaped the ≤3-met definition the authors propose. NRG-LU002 is the phase III test of the question.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents oligometastatic (≤3 mets) NSCLC stable or responding after platinum doublet or first-line EGFR/ALK TKI. Does not represent immunotherapy-treated pts, >3 mets, or disease progressing on front-line therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Early stopping for benefit tends to overstate the effect size. Maintenance regimens were heterogeneous, so an LCT x systemic-therapy interaction cannot be detected. The **EGFR/ALK subgroup (n=8)** is too small to interpret.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The OS benefit appears despite crossover, which points to **timing** rather than receipt of LCT: consolidating before progression beats waiting, because many pts become polymetastatic and lose eligibility. **Whether this holds with IO maintenance is unsettled.**

studies.interpretation:
The trial's lasting contribution is not the PFS result, which was already published and is close to what one expects when all visible disease is treated locally. It is the overall survival separation, observed in a design that let control-arm pts cross over to local therapy at progression. Crossover usually dilutes an OS difference. That a gap of 41.2 vs 17.0 mo median OS persisted suggests the benefit is tied to when consolidation happens, not just whether it ever happens. The survival-after-progression data support this. Pts originally assigned to LCT lived 37.6 mo after progression vs 9.4 mo in the MT/O arm, and fewer than half of progressing pts could receive comprehensive local therapy at that point, mostly because they had become polymetastatic. For the radiation oncologist, the window after first-line induction looks like the moment when ablating every site is still feasible, and the opportunity may close.

Methodology should temper confidence in the magnitude more than in the direction. The trial randomized 49 pts against a planned 94 and stopped on a DSMB efficacy look. Truncated trials systematically overestimate effect sizes, and the design used a one-sided 10% type I error, a phase II threshold that is not a confirmatory standard. OS was a secondary endpoint with wide intervals (LCT 18.9 mo to not reached). Assignment was unmasked, although indexing imaging to enrollment in both arms removed one common source of PFS bias in local-therapy trials. The adjusted HR of 0.46 with an upper bound of 0.99 sits just inside the conventional line, so modest prognostic imbalance in a trial this size could move it.

In context, the result aligns with the randomized phase II literature that made consolidation a recognized option, including SABR-COMET and the UT Southwestern trial. The authors explicitly lean on those trials to support a ≤3-metastasis definition that is not restricted by molecular profile. The magnitude in a less selected population is probably smaller. These pts had already shown biology favorable enough to remain stable on first-line therapy for at least three months, and most had synchronous disease and adenocarcinoma histology.

The largest transferability gap is immunotherapy. The trial opened in 2012, its control arm received chemotherapy-era maintenance, and the median OS in the MT/O arm reflects that era. Against a modern IO backbone the control arm would likely live longer, and the absolute gain from consolidation could shrink, or it could interact with IO in either direction. Nothing here addresses that. The trial also does not report RT dose or the split between surgery and radiation, so it informs whether to consolidate, not how.

The result would be wrong if early stopping caught a random high or if dynamic balancing left residual confounding on unmeasured burden. NRG-LU002 is the test that resolves both. Until then, this is the strongest randomized argument for treating the post-induction window as the decision point, applied to the population the trial actually enrolled.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Only 41% of progressors could receive LCT at progression, and survival after progression was 37.6 vs 9.4 mo, so the post-induction window is the RT decision point. Dose and fractionation are not reported in the source, so the trial informs whether to consolidate, not the prescription.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Maintenance or observation alone after platinum doublet or first-line TKI gave mOS 17.0 vs 41.2 mo with LCT. That argues for referring stable ≤3-met pts for consolidation before progression. The control backbone predates immunotherapy, so the effect on top of IO maintenance is unknown.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Surgery was an allowed LCT modality, chosen by the MDT, with the same intent of treating all active sites. The source does not report how many pts were resected or any surgical outcomes, so the data support consolidation as a strategy without separating resection from RT.

sites.intro: In resected HPV+ OPSCC (NCDB), margins and nodal size/laterality lose prognostic weight, and those features are the classic triggers for adjuvant RT/CRT.

studies.name: Composite pathologic risk stratification, resected HPV+ oropharyngeal cancer
studies.tldr: Composite point score raised C-index from 0.58 to 0.67 in resected HPV+ OPSCC; low-risk share rose from 24.5% to 75.3% (NCDB, n=2302).
details: 🔍 Retrospective NCDB cohort, dx 2010-2013, primary surgery plus neck dissection with LN yield ≥15
🔍 2302 HPV+ OPSCC; 13 022 HPV-unassociated HNSCC as the contrast cohort
📊 Traditional (NCCN/ASCO/ECOG 3311/PATHOS-derived) risk C-index 0.58 in HPV+ OPSCC vs 0.68 in HPV-unassociated HNSCC

details.text: 🔍 Composite score: adverse points per pathologic feature (low 0-3, intermediate 4-5, high ≥6 points)

rows: T1-2 · tonsil or BOT · 0-1 metastatic LNs · any LN size · level IV or V LNs · bilateral LN · differentiation
LVI · microscopically positive margins · microscopic ENE
T3 · 2-4 metastatic LNs · grossly positive margins · macroscopic ENE

details: 📊 Composite C-index 0.67 with 3 risk groups, 0.73 using individual points

details.text: 📊 Reclassification in HPV+ OPSCC, traditional → composite

details: 📊 HPV+ multivariable: only T stage, LVI, number of metastatic LNs and ENE tracked with mortality
📊 Not prognostic in HPV+: surgical margins, LN size, level IV-V nodes, bilateral/contralateral nodes
⚠️ Cox models adjusted for adjuvant RT/CRT, which margins and ENE themselves triggered; treated risk can look benign
⚠️ OS is the only endpoint; NCDB carries no locoregional recurrence, PNI, close margins or smoking
⚠️ Score derived and scored in the same cohort; no external validation reported in source
⚠️ High-risk traditional share reported as 46.1% (n=1061) in Results but 45.1% (n=1038) in Discussion

verdict.rationale: Registry-derived prognostic score, OS-only, no external validation; feature HRs adjusted for the adjuvant therapy those same features prompted, so de-escalation cannot be inferred.
verdict.audience: Resected HPV+ OPSCC with neck dissection (≥15 nodes), AJCC 7th

studies.significance: The score demotes the classic CRT triggers: margin status lost prognostic weight in HPV+ disease on multivariable analysis, and microscopic ENE earns one point, so a T1-2 tumour with microscopic ENE can still sit low-risk. That points at adjuvant RT/CRT de-escalation, but those HRs were measured after the adjuvant therapy the features prompted.
studies.monday_clinic: In resected HPV+ OPSCC with microscopic ENE or a microscopically positive margin, this questions whether those features carry the prognostic weight that drives adjuvant CRT, as a hypothesis only; it does not extend to HPV-unassociated HNSCC or replace ECOG 3311/PATHOS trial risk definitions.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Retrospective NCDB cohort**, diagnoses 2010-2013, analysed 2018-2019. Points assigned to features in proportion to univariate and multivariable Cox effect size, then the composite chosen by **C-index, AIC and clinical judgement**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Nonmetastatic HNSCC (T1-4, N0-3, M0) with **definitive primary surgery and neck dissection yielding ≥15 nodes**. **2302 HPV+ OPSCC** vs 13 022 HPV-unassociated HNSCC; untested OPSCC and surgery plus chemo alone excluded.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary: 5-year OS** (Kaplan-Meier, log-rank) and discrimination by **concordance index**. Multivariable models adjusted for age, sex, race, comorbidity, insurance, adjuvant RT/CRT and hospital type.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Traditional stratification discriminated poorly in HPV+ OPSCC (**C-index 0.58** vs 0.68 in HPV-unassociated). Composite reached **0.67** (3 groups) and **0.73** (points), moving low-risk from **24.5% to 75.3%** and high-risk from **45.1% to 6.6%**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Traditional definitions here derive from NCCN, ASCO, **ECOG 3311** and **PATHOS**, which differ on ENE extent and nodal count thresholds. **ICON-S** refined HPV+ staging but only 2% of its pts were surgical, so it could not test pathologic features.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents surgically resected HPV+ OPSCC with adequate neck dissection, staged AJCC 7th. Does not represent HPV-unassociated HNSCC, pts managed with definitive CRT, or features NCDB lacks (PNI, close margins, smoking).

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: **Adjustment for adjuvant RT/CRT** means margins and ENE are scored after the therapy they triggered, biasing them toward null. **OS only**: no locoregional control, the endpoint an adjuvant RT decision actually turns on. High-risk share is reported inconsistently (46.1% vs 45.1%).

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The score reframes HPV+ pathologic risk around **tumour burden (T stage, nodal count)** rather than margins and ENE extent. It is a **hypothesis for deintensification trials**, not a basis for omitting adjuvant therapy, until tested on recurrence in an independent cohort.

studies.interpretation:
The core finding is that the pathologic risk grammar built for HPV-unassociated head and neck cancer barely discriminates survival once the tumour is HPV-associated. A C-index of 0.58 is close to a coin flip, and the contrast with 0.68 in the HPV-unassociated cohort, scored with the same rules in the same registry, makes the point cleanly. That part of the paper is the most defensible, because it does not depend on the new score at all: it is a direct test of the existing framework, and it agrees with the surgical series the authors cite showing diminished weight for margins, ENE and LVI in HPV+ disease.

The composite score itself deserves less confidence than its headline suggests. It was derived and evaluated on the same 2302 patients, selected partly on C-index and AIC, so 0.67 and 0.73 are apparent performance and will shrink in an independent cohort. More importantly for a radiation oncologist, the multivariable models adjusted for adjuvant RT and CRT. In this era, a positive margin or ENE was the reason a patient received CRT. Measuring the prognostic weight of those features after conditioning on the treatment they triggered estimates their residual risk once treated, not their untreated risk. A margin that looks non-prognostic may simply be a margin that chemoradiation neutralised. That is the opposite of the question a de-escalation decision asks, which is what happens if the treatment is withheld.

The endpoint compounds this. NCDB records death, not recurrence, and HPV+ OPSCC carries high salvage rates and long post-recurrence survival. Adjuvant RT is justified primarily by locoregional control, and an OS-only analysis in a disease with good salvage is poorly equipped to detect the locoregional cost of a weaker adjuvant plan. The absence of perineural invasion, close margins and smoking from the model also matters, since smoking in particular modifies HPV+ prognosis and was not available to adjust for.

Against the trials that frame current practice, the score is closest in spirit to PATHOS and ECOG 3311, which already moved toward risk-adapted adjuvant intensity after transoral surgery, and to ICON-S, which re-weighted HPV+ staging for nonsurgical patients. Its distinct contribution is shifting the weight toward tumour and nodal burden: T3-4 and nodal count carry the most points, while microscopic ENE and microscopically positive margins carry one each. Under that scheme a tumour with LVI, microscopic ENE and a microscopically positive margin still falls inside the low-risk band, a patient most radiation oncologists would currently treat with CRT. The reclassification from 45.1% high-risk to 6.6% is therefore not a refinement but a large reallocation, and its safety rests entirely on the treatment-confounded HRs above.

The right reading is that this paper supports designing trials that randomise adjuvant intensity within composite-defined low-risk groups, with locoregional recurrence as the endpoint. It does not support omitting or de-intensifying adjuvant CRT for ENE or margin status in routine practice. For it to be wrong, an untreated or lightly treated cohort would need to show that microscopic ENE and positive margins do carry meaningful locoregional risk, which is precisely what the adjustment here cannot exclude.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Margins lost prognostic weight in HPV+ disease and microscopic ENE earns one point, so classic CRT triggers can land low-risk. That points toward adjuvant RT/CRT de-escalation, but HRs were adjusted for the adjuvant therapy those features prompted, and OS cannot capture locoregional cost.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: After transoral resection with ≥15-node dissection, nodal count and T stage carried prognostic weight while margin status, LN size, level IV-V and bilateral nodes did not on multivariable analysis. Adequate nodal yield is the entry condition, so the score is only applicable after a complete neck dissection.

papers.title: Local Consolidative Therapy Vs. Maintenance Therapy or Observation for Patients With Oligometastatic Non–Small-Cell Lung Cancer: Long-Term Results of a Multi-Institutional, Phase II, Randomized Study
papers.abstract: PURPOSE Our previously published findings reported that local consolidative therapy (LCT) with radiotherapy or surgery improved progression-free survival (PFS) and delayed new disease in patients with oligometastatic non–small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that did not progress after front-line systemic therapy. Herein, we present the longer-term overall survival (OS) results accompanied by additional secondary end points. PATIENTS AND METHODS This multicenter, randomized, phase II trial enrolled patients with stage IV NSCLC, three or fewer metastases, and no progression at 3 or more months after front-line systemic therapy. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to maintenance therapy or observation (MT/O) or to LCT to all active disease sites. The primary end point was PFS; secondary end points were OS, toxicity, and the appearance of new lesions. All analyses were two sided, and P values less than .10 were deemed significant. RESULTS The Data Safety and Monitoring Board recommended early trial closure after 49 patients were randomly assigned because of a significant PFS benefit in the LCT arm. With an updated median follow-up time of 38.8 months (range, 28.3 to 61.4 months), the PFS benefit was durable (median, 14.2 months [95% CI, 7.4 to 23.1 months] with LCT v 4.4 months [95% CI, 2.2 to 8.3 months] with MT/O; P = .022). We also found an OS benefit in the LCT arm (median, 41.2 months [95% CI, 18.9 months to not reached] with LCT v 17.0 months [95% CI, 10.1 to 39.8 months] with MT/O; P = .017). No additional grade 3 or greater toxicities were observed. Survival after progression was longer in the LCT group (37.6 months with LCT v 9.4 months with MT/O; P = .034). Of the 20 patients who experienced progression in the MT/O arm, nine received LCT to all lesions after progression, and the median OS was 17 months (95% CI, 7.8 months to not reached). CONCLUSION In patients with oligometastatic NSCLC that did not progress after front-line systemic therapy, LCT prolonged PFS and OS relative to MT/O.

papers.title: Postoperative endometrial cancer treatments with electronic brachytherapy source
papers.abstract: Abstract Purpose This study is a dosimetric and acute toxicity comparison of endometrial cancer patients treated with either Axxent (Xoft, Inc., San José, CA, USA) electronic and interstitial brachytherapy versus interstitial high dose rate brachytherapy (HDRBT). Materials and Methods Between 2015 and 2017, 94 patients with postoperative endometrial cancer were treated in our centre with the Axxent electronic brachytherapy (eBT) system. The V 150 and V 200 are evaluated prospectively for each plan. The mean age of patients was 65.9 years (age range 33–84 years), with different tumour staging. Of the 94 patients, 37 received exclusive adjuvant brachytherapy (25 Gy in five sessions); the remaining patients received external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) with a regimen of 23 sessions of 2 Gy each to the entire pelvis, followed by eBT (15 Gy in three sessions). Additionally, the absorbed doses received by the organs at risk (OAR), urinary bladder, rectum and sigmoid colon were compared with HDRBT plans, evaluating D 2cc , V 50% and V 35% . Median follow-up was done for each of the 94 patients to assess the toxicity of the treatment: vaginal mucosa toxicity, rectal and urinary toxicity; and results are presented for acute toxicity, toxicity at 1 month after the end of treatment and follow-up after 12 months for a portion of patients according to the Radiation Therapy Oncology Group (RTOG) toxicity criteria. Results The doses in OAR for eBT plans were lower than that for HDRBT plans, both Ir-192 and Co-60 plans, whose doses were similar. The dose in bladder with eBT was 63.8% of the prescribed dose for D 2cc versus 70.1% for HDRBT Ir-192, for V 50% was 7.2% versus 12.7% and for V 35% was 15.2% versus 28.2%. In rectum the D 2cc was 61.2% versus 68.4%, for V 50% was 7.9% versus 14.3% and for V 35% was 16.7% versus 32%. Results demonstrated lower doses to OAR in all eBT plans. Acute toxicity in eBT was very low in cases of mucositis, with only one case of toxicity greater than grade 1, rectal toxicity and urinary toxicity; results at 1 month are equally good, toxicity symptoms disappeared and no relapses have occurred to date. Conclusions The results of treatment with the Axxent eBT unit for 94 patients are very good, as no recurrence has been observed and the toxicity of the treatment is very low. The increase in V 150 and V 200 has not produced an increase in vaginal mucosa toxicity, and the doses in the OAR are lower than in the plans implemented for HDRBT with Ir-192 or Co-60. eBT is a good alternative to treat endometrial cancer in centres without conventional HDR availability. To date, there are limited published studies reporting on outcomes from patients treated with eBT.
